subtopics.title: Carpentry, joinery and the classes of tools
subtopics.theory_md:
**Carpentry** is cutting, shaping and joining timber for rough structural work (frames, roofs, doors). **Joinery** is the finer work of making joints for furniture, shutters and panelling.

Tools are classified by job:
- **Marking and measuring**: steel rule, tape, try square, marking gauge, mortise gauge, sliding bevel, scriber.
- **Holding**: carpenter's vice, bench hook, G-clamp, sash clamp.
- **Cutting**: saws, chisels.
- **Planing**: jack, smoothing, trying, rebate, plough plane.
- **Boring**: brace and bit, auger, gimlet, bradawl.
- **Striking**: claw hammer, mallet.
- **Miscellaneous**: rasp, file, screwdriver, pincers, oilstone.
subtopics.basics_md: Every job in wood needs the same few things: mark where to cut, hold the wood still, cut it, smooth it, drill it, hit things, and finish it. The tool groups follow those jobs.
key_points: Carpentry = rough structural wooden work; joinery = fine jointed work
Seven classes: marking and measuring, holding, cutting, planing, boring, striking, miscellaneous
Give two named examples per class
Try square checks right angles; bevel sets any angle

subtopics.title: Marking, measuring and holding tools
subtopics.theory_md:
**Marking gauge**: stock sliding on a stem with **one pin**; scribes a line parallel to an edge, along the grain.
**Mortise gauge**: **two pins**, one adjustable; marks both sides of a mortise or tenon in one stroke.
**Try square**: stock and blade at 90 degrees; checks squareness and marks lines across the grain.
**Sliding bevel**: adjustable blade; sets and transfers any angle, e.g. 45 degrees for a mitre.
**Steel rule, tape**: lengths. **Scriber or pencil** for lines.

**Holding**: carpenter's vice (on the bench), bench hook (stops the job when sawing), G-clamp, sash (bar) clamp for gluing frames, hand vice.
subtopics.basics_md: To cut accurately you first draw a line you trust and then stop the wood from moving. Marking tools draw the line; holding tools stop the movement.

Try square: right angles; sliding bevel: any angle

subtopics.title: Saws
subtopics.theory_md:
**Rip saw**: cuts **along the grain**; coarse, about 4 to 6 teeth per 25 mm; teeth filed square (chisel-edged) and chop out the fibres.
**Cross-cut saw**: cuts **across the grain**; finer, about 7 to 10 teeth per 25 mm; teeth filed with a bevel (knife-edged) that sever the fibres on both sides of the kerf.
**Tenon (back) saw**: stiff back, fine teeth; accurate cuts in joints.
**Dovetail saw**: finer tenon saw. **Coping saw**: thin blade in a U-frame, curves in thin wood. **Keyhole or compass saw**: narrow tapered blade, internal and curved cuts. **Bow saw**, and power **circular** and **band saw**.

Saw on the waste side of the line.
subtopics.basics_md: Along the grain you are splitting fibres apart, so you want chisels. Across the grain you must cut fibres through, so you want knives.
key_points: Rip saw: along the grain, coarse, chisel teeth
Cross-cut saw: across the grain, finer, knife-edged teeth
Tenon saw for joints (stiff back); coping and keyhole saws for curves and holes

questions.q: Why must a cross-cut saw have knife-edged teeth, while a rip saw has chisel-edged teeth?
questions.model_answer_md: Across the grain the fibres must be **severed** on both sides of the cut, which knife-edged (bevel-filed) teeth do cleanly. Along the grain the fibres only have to be **chiselled out** in a line, which square-filed teeth do fast, so a rip saw cuts quickly but roughly.

Rip: chisel teeth remove fibres along the grain

subtopics.title: Planes, chisels, boring and striking tools
subtopics.theory_md:
**Jack plane** (350 to 400 mm, general planing). Parts: **body with flat sole**, **mouth**, **cutting iron** (blade, bedded at about 45 degrees), **cap iron** (back iron: stiffens the blade and breaks the shaving so the grain does not tear), **lever cap**, adjusting nut and lateral lever, handle, knob.
**Smoothing plane**: short, final finish. **Trying (jointer) plane**: long, true long edges. **Rebate plane**: steps. **Plough plane**: grooves.
**Chisels**: firmer (general), bevel-edge (fine, dovetails), mortise (thick, chopping), struck with a **wooden mallet**.
**Boring**: bradawl, gimlet, brace and bit, auger. **Claw hammer** drives and pulls nails.
subtopics.basics_md: A plane is a chisel held in a block so it takes the same thin shaving every pass. A longer block (trying plane) rides over hollows and makes a straighter edge.
key_points: Jack plane parts: sole, mouth, cutting iron at 45 degrees, cap iron, lever cap, adjusting nut, handle, knob

questions.model_answer_md:

subtopics.title: Structure of a timber tree
subtopics.theory_md:
Timber comes from **exogenous** trees, which grow outward by adding a ring each year. Cross-section from the centre outward:
1. **Pith**: soft central core.
2. **Heartwood**: dark, dense, dead inner rings; strong and durable; the timber.
3. **Sapwood**: light outer rings carrying sap; weaker, decays easily.
4. **Cambium**: thin layer that makes new wood and bark.
5. **Inner bark (bast)**: carries food down.
6. **Outer bark**: protects.

**Annual rings**: one per year, count gives age. **Medullary rays**: radial lines from pith to bark; store and carry food sideways.
subtopics.basics_md: A tree grows a new skin of wood under the bark every year, like layers of an onion. Old inner layers stop carrying sap and become hard heartwood.
key_points: Sketch circle: pith, heartwood, sapwood, cambium, inner bark, outer bark
Annual rings give the age; medullary rays are radial

subtopics.title: Seasoning of timber
subtopics.theory_md:
**Seasoning** removes moisture from green timber (40 to 60 per cent water) down to **10 to 15 per cent** (8 to 12 for furniture).

**Why**: stops later shrinkage, warping and cracking; raises strength and durability; lighter; resists fungi and insects; easier to work, glue and polish.

**Natural (air)**: planks stacked on raised bearers with spacers in a shaded, ventilated shed; cheap, slow (months to years).
**Artificial**: **kiln** (hot humid air, about 35 to 40 degrees C rising to 60 to 80, days), water, boiling or steaming, chemical (urea, salt), electrical (high frequency).

Moisture content $MC=\dfrac{W_{wet}-W_{dry}}{W_{dry}}\times100$ (oven-dry basis).
subtopics.basics_md: Fresh wood is full of water. It shrinks as it dries, and if it dries after being made into a door, the door cracks. So we dry it first, slowly and evenly.
key_points: Seasoning = controlled removal of moisture to 10 to 15 per cent
Purpose: no warping or cracking, more strength and durability, resists fungi and insects
Natural: stacked in shade, slow, cheap; artificial: kiln, water, boiling, chemical, electrical
Kiln: fast, controlled; start humid, raise temperature, then condition

subtopics.title: Defects in timber and choosing good timber
subtopics.theory_md:
**Natural defects**: **knots** (branch bases, weaken and break the grain), **shakes** (cracks along the grain: heart, star, cup, ring, radial), cross or spiral grain, rind galls, upsets, burls.
**Seasoning defects**: **warping** (bow, cup, twist), **checks and splits**, honeycombing, case hardening; also **wane** (bark or rounded edge).
**Decay**: dry rot, wet rot, fungal stain; **insects**: borers, termites.

Effect: lower strength, poor finish, weak joints, wastage, short life.

**Good timber**: straight uniform close grain; hard, strong, heavy; durable; well seasoned; free from defects; easy to work, takes polish; dark uniform colour; clear ring when struck. Selection also depends on use, cost and availability.
subtopics.basics_md: Wood is a natural material, so it has flaws: places where a branch grew, cracks from drying, and rot. A good carpenter learns to spot them before cutting.

subtopics.title: Nails, screws and bolts
subtopics.theory_md:
**Nails** (mild steel wire): wire nail (round head), oval (less splitting), cut nail, clout (flat head, roofing felt), panel pin or lost-head (head punched below the surface), brad. Specified by **length and gauge**. Drive slightly inclined for grip; keep off the ends to avoid splitting.

**Wood screws**: countersunk (flush), round head, raised head; slotted or Phillips. Specified by **length and gauge number**. Drill a **pilot hole** (smaller than the root diameter) and a clearance hole in the top piece. Screws hold better than nails and can be removed.

**Carriage bolt** (round head, square neck) and **coach screw** (square head, spanner) for heavy work. **Corrugated fasteners** for butt and mitre joints.
subtopics.basics_md: A nail grips by friction; a screw has a thread that bites, so it holds more and can be unwound. The pilot hole makes room so the wood does not split.
key_points: Nails: wire, oval, cut, clout, panel pin, brad; length and gauge

subtopics.title: Basic operations and the order of work
subtopics.theory_md:
**Order of work**: select seasoned timber, **mark**, **saw**, **plane**, **chisel**, **bore**, **assemble**, **finish**.

- **Face side and face edge** are planed first, flat and square to each other, and marked with face marks; all other marking is done from them.
- **Marking**: gauge and try square from the face side and edge.
- **Sawing**: ripping along the grain, cross-cutting across; saw in the waste side of the line.
- **Planing**: with the grain, to width and thickness.
- **Chiselling**: **paring** (thin slices by hand pressure) and **chopping** (mallet, mortises).
- Also boring, grooving, rebating, chamfering, sanding.
subtopics.basics_md: A cut is only as accurate as the line it follows, and the line is only accurate if it was measured from a true flat surface. That surface is the face side.

Face side and face edge first; mark all dimensions from them
Saw on the waste side; plane with the grain

**Face side and edge** are planed flat and square to each other. They are the datum, so width, thickness, shoulders and mortises are gauged from them and every piece comes out consistent and square. Face marks stop them being confused.

**Paring**: removing thin shavings with the chisel pushed by hand pressure. **Chopping**: striking the chisel with a mallet to cut deeper, as in a mortise.

subtopics.title: Wood joints: construction, use, advantages
subtopics.theory_md:
| Joint | Construction | Use | Advantage |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Lap (halving)**: cross, T, corner | Half thickness removed from each piece, faces flush | Frames, stretchers | Simple, flat, good glue area |
| **Mortise and tenon** | Tenon (about one-third of the thickness) fits a mortise; pinned or wedged | Doors, windows, table legs | Strongest frame joint, resists racking |
| **Bridle** | Open slot receives a tongue | Frames, legs | Strong, easy |
| **Dovetail** | Tails interlock with pins, slope 1:6 soft, 1:8 hard | Drawers, boxes | Locks, resists pull |
| **Mitre** | Both ends at 45 degrees | Picture frames | Hidden end grain |
| **Dowel** | Round pins in matching holes | Panels, table tops | Hidden, aligned |
| **Butt** | End to face, nailed or glued | Boxes | Cheapest |
| **Tongue and groove** | Tongue in groove | Flooring, panelling | Tight, flat |
subtopics.basics_md: Every joint trades effort for strength. A butt joint is the easiest and weakest; mortise and tenon and dovetail take work but lock the pieces mechanically.
key_points: Lap joint: half the thickness from each piece, flush faces
Mortise and tenon: tenon about one-third of the stock thickness; strongest frame joint
Dovetail: interlocking tails and pins, for drawers; resists pulling apart

Dovetail angle $=\tan^{-1}(1/6)=9.46^\circ$ (about $9.5^\circ$ from the vertical edge).

subtopics.title: Steps to make a joint
subtopics.theory_md:
**Mortise and tenon**:
1. Select seasoned timber; plane to size and square.
2. **Mark** with the mortise gauge from the face side; shoulder lines with try square and knife.
3. **Cut the tenon**: clamp in the vice, saw the cheeks along the grain, then the shoulders across the grain.
4. **Cut the mortise**: bore a row of holes inside the lines, or chop with mortise chisel and mallet; pare the walls.
5. **Fit** and trim, check square.
6. **Assemble**: glue, push home, peg or wedge, clamp, clean, plane and sand.

**Cross or L halving**: mark width and half depth on both pieces, saw shoulders and cheeks to the depth line (in the waste), chisel out the waste, test fit.
subtopics.basics_md: Making a joint is marking exactly, sawing short of the line, then paring to fit. Test fit before gluing.
key_points: Mark from face side with gauge and try square
Tenon cheeks along the grain, shoulders across, with tenon saw
Mortise by boring a row of holes or chopping, then paring
Test fit, glue, peg or wedge, clamp, finish
Halving: saw to half depth, chisel out waste

**Steps**

2. Mark mortise and tenon with the mortise gauge from the face side; shoulders with try square.
3. Saw tenon cheeks (along the grain) and shoulders (across) with the tenon saw.
4. Cut the mortise: bore holes with brace and bit, chop with mortise chisel and mallet, pare walls.

subtopics.title: Planning a whole job: door, cot, table
subtopics.theory_md:
A job question has four parts: **figure**, **joints**, **tools**, **operations**.

**Panelled door**: vertical stiles; top, middle (lock) and bottom rails; panels in grooves. Joints: **mortise and tenon** (haunched at the top rail) for stile to rail, **tongue and groove** or rebate for the panel, **butt** for hinge leaves, **mitre** for mouldings.
**Cot**: four legs, two long side rails, two short rails; **mortise and tenon** at each leg, dowel or bridle alternatives, halving for cross-bracing.
**Study table**: legs and aprons by mortise and tenon, top fixed by buttons or screws, **dovetail** for the drawer.

Operations: season, mark, saw, plane, chisel, dry fit, glue and clamp, finish.

subtopics.title: Personal protection and shop housekeeping
subtopics.theory_md:
**Personal**: apron and close-fitting clothes; no loose sleeves, ties or jewellery; tie long hair; safety shoes; **goggles** for chiselling, sanding and machine work; dust mask when sanding.
**Shop**: floor free of shavings (slips and fire); no smoking or flames near wood dust and finishes; fire extinguisher and first-aid box within reach; report every injury; no horseplay.
subtopics.basics_md: Most shop accidents come from loose clothing, flying chips, slippery floors and fire. The rules just remove those causes.

subtopics.title: Safe use of hand tools and machines
subtopics.theory_md:
- Keep tools **sharp**: a blunt tool needs force and slips.
- Never use a chisel or file without a **handle**; strike chisels with a **mallet**.
- Cut **away from the body**, both hands **behind the cutting edge**.
- Hold the work in a vice, bench hook or clamp.
- Lay planes **on the side** (or retract the blade); carry sharp tools pointing down; never in pockets.
- Check timber for **nails** before sawing or planing.
- **Machines**: use guards, push sticks for short pieces, never adjust while running, switch off and wait until the cutter stops, one operator, know the emergency stop.
subtopics.basics_md: A slipping tool follows the push of your hand. Make sure the path it would take is empty: hands behind the edge, work clamped, edge away from the body.
key_points: Sharp tools safer than blunt ones
Hands behind the edge, cut away from the body
Plane on its side, tools carried pointing down
Check for nails; clamp the work
Machines: guards, push stick, switch off before adjusting

questions.q: Why is a sharp tool safer than a blunt one, and why must timber be checked for nails before planing or sawing?
questions.model_answer_md:
A **sharp tool** cuts with little force and stays under control; a blunt one needs extra force, skids and can slip into the hand.

 A hidden **nail** chips or breaks the plane iron or saw teeth and can make the tool jerk or throw fragments, injuring the worker.
